data.title: Zámčisko near Nová Baňa – a massive hillfort below Veľký Inovec
data.excerpt: Roughly 10 km west of Nová Baňa, on a steep hill at 690 m above sea level below Veľký Inovec, lies the hillfort of Zámčisko, defended by an earthen rampart 430 m long reinforced on the inner side by a firm ring of stone. A short evaluation excavation in 1970 and 1971 assigned its pottery to the 10th–13th centuries and showed Slavic occupation, probably of refuge character, on a fortified settlement established in prehistory.

timeline.title: Survey of the hillfort

timeline.title: Evaluation excavation

timeline.title: Slavic occupation of the hillfort
timeline.description: The pottery finds from the uncovered features belong typologically to the 10th–13th centuries and attest to an original Slavic occupation of refuge character in the Early Middle Ages, on an already existing fortified settlement established in prehistory.

timeline.title: The founding of Nová Baňa
timeline.description: According to a view widespread until recently, the surroundings of Nová Baňa were occupied only from the founding of the town at the time of the colonisation by German settlers in the 14th century – the excavation of the hillfort, however, refuted this idea.

children.text: Roughly 10 km west of Nová Baňa (Žiar nad Hronom district), above the hamlets of Stará Huta and Bukovina, the archaeological site of Zámčisko extends over a steep hill (690 m above sea level) below the highest peak of the Pohronský Inovec mountains – Veľký Inovec (900 m above sea level). An earthen rampart 430 m long, reinforced on the inner side by a firm ring of stone, attests to a massive fortification system which on the northern side joins a 200 m long defensive line created by the favourable configuration of the terrain. In places, over longer stretches, the earthen rampart passes into a stone construction. The massive rampart ensured the protection of the whole enclosure of the hillfort, with its undulating terrain, covering an area of about 7 ha and cleft into two unequal parts by a longitudinal andesite rock formation running north–south.

The hillfort has a strategically very advantageous position, since it is difficult to reach, offers a good view eastwards into the Hron region and allows key protection of the narrow pass through which the road towards Veľká Lehota runs – a road probably used from time immemorial as a connecting route from the upper Žitava region to the middle Hron region.

This important archaeological site, situated high in the Pohronský Inovec mountains, was already known to Hungarian archaeologists in the 19th century. In 1869 the Nová Baňa town mining and forestry engineer Ján Flakovits surveyed the hillfort and drew up a site plan of it. The collections of the Town Museum in Nová Baňa hold a variety of finds recovered in the second half of the last century (a small bronze axe, iron spurs, horseshoes and sherds), which are thought perhaps to come from the enclosure of Zámčisko.

In 1970 and 1971 a short-term evaluation excavation was carried out at the site, the aim of which was to gain insights into the character of the occupation of the hillfort at Zámčisko. During this excavation the 430 m long rampart was surveyed again, as was the position of the andesite rock formation which cuts across the hillfort and divides it into a higher western and a lower eastern part. The rock formation is interrupted by the narrow pass mentioned above, through which the road runs. The enclosure of the hillfort is very uneven and covered with fairly dense woodland (firs, beeches). The height of the rampart at the best-preserved point is more than 250 cm, and the ditch reaches a depth of 150 cm in places.

children.text: Fifteen trenches were dug, three features were uncovered and a section was also cut through the rampart. In the western part of the hillfort, in the immediate vicinity of the rampart (on its inner side), the remains survived of walls 40–45 cm thick and 110 cm high belonging to a building of almost square plan measuring 250 × 260 cm, built of flat fragments of andesite from the local rock formation, drystone-laid. In the immediate vicinity of the outer side of the rampart, traces were found of the stone foundations of two similar buildings of roughly the same plan, placed on both sides of a break in the rampart. This situation tempts one to suppose that these are the foundations of tower-like guard structures of log construction on both sides of the original entrance into the enclosure of the hillfort.

In the trenches in which the remains of the collapsed structures of settlement features were uncovered – features situated on small terraced platforms, especially near the ramparts – circular hearths stood out more clearly, and pottery sherds were recovered. Typologically this pottery can be assigned to the 10th–13th centuries.

Particular attention was devoted to the construction of the rampart. It had the following composition: homogeneous red clay, in places cemented – as if fused – into lumps of fired clay. At a depth of 180 cm the red clay gradually began to mix with dark-coloured soil. Here, in the middle of the section, a continuous layer of stones 20–30 cm high and 60–70 cm wide was found at the bottom, running parallel to the line of the crest of the rampart. This is undoubtedly the stone core of the foundation of the rampart construction, laid on the surface before the digging of the ditch and the gradual piling up of the rampart. In the deeper layers of the ditch similar red soil appeared, of which the rampart is built along about half of its length (below Zámčisko there is a small hamlet called Červené zeme, and the same brick-red clay occurs there). In the remaining part of the rampart a stone construction without this clay predominates. Traces of charcoal, which appeared as the section through the rampart was deepened both vertically and horizontally, also point to a probable timber construction. In the part in which red clay was used as the main building material (possibly in combination with timber), the rampart is reinforced along its whole length on the inner side by a thick ring of stone facing, in places up to a height of 150 cm and with a maximum width at the base of up to 100 cm. The stone facing then merges with the rest of the construction, in which fragments of andesite were used as the building material.

Beneath a vertical fissure in the rock formation the archaeologists discovered a water source now gone, attested by the unusual modification of the terrain and the constant dampness of its surroundings.

The results of the evaluation excavation convincingly refute the tendentious views, widespread until recently, that the surroundings of Nová Baňa were occupied only from the founding of the town more than six and a quarter centuries ago – at the time of the colonisation by German settlers in the 14th century. The results obtained so far from the short-term evaluation excavation of the hillfort cannot fully explain the reasons for occupation in such an inaccessible place, with the unusually undulating surface of the hillfort enclosure. They do, however, attest to an original Slavic occupation, probably of refuge character, in the Early Middle Ages (10th–13th centuries), that is, in the period of the emerging and gradually consolidating Hungarian state, and that on an already existing fortified settlement established in prehistory.
